newsitem.title: SPAIN: JOBS-Spain's jobless to find little solace in EMU.
newsitem.headline: JOBS-Spain's jobless to find little solace in EMU.

text.p: Spain hopes that membership of Europe's proposed common currency bloc will help dent its lengthy queues of unemployed, but analysts say an uphill battle looms.
In a continent burdened by joblessness, Spain bears by far the heaviest load with unemployment running at more than 20 percent, double the European average.

The conservative Popular Party government is banking on the single currency to boost growth and help put people back to work, but economists worry Spain's economy is too rigid to benefit, or even to withstand the strain.
"Entrance into European economic and monetary union will undoubtedly be positive for employment," Spanish Employment Secretary Manuel Pimentel Siles told Reuters.

"The establishment of a single currency carries with it free movement and transparency of capital, while loans and financing costs should improve and have a medium-term effect over the economy's productive base," Pimentel said.
But the economy growth which Spain would need to reduce unemployment even to the European standard far exceeds anything expected from the single currency launch foreseen in 1999.

"The rule of thumb is that Spain needs five percent growth each year for a decade to reduce its unemployment to the European average," said Juan Dolado of the Economy Department of Madrid's Carlos III university.
LABOUR FRAMEWORK A FRANCO LEGACY
Spain's heavy unemployment is in large part a legacy of fascist dictator Francisco Franco, who died in 1975, having set up a labour framework that gave workers near total security.

While this presented no problems during periods of economi expansion, as growth slowed high dismissal costs discouraged employment and pushed joblessness up steadily to a peak of 24.2 percent in 1994, according to the National Statistics Institute's (INE).
The rate -- based on household surveys and considered the most reliable indicators -- has since eased to 21.78 percent.

But despite reforms in 1984 and in 1994, the labour market is still rigid. Dismissal costs remain excessive, unemployment benefits are long-lived and labour movements around the country are restricted.
In the past, Spain compensated for dwindling growth with boosts via competitive devaluations of the peseta, the last of which took place in the spring of 1995.
But the single currency will end that option.

"We have to clean up our own house as economic activity goes up and down," said Henrik Lumholdt, economist at Bank of America in Madrid. "If we don't do anything then that inflexibility is going to be transformed into fiscal problems."

The government has urged unions and employers to reach agreement to liberalise the market and warned in late February that it would step in and force an accord if the two sides could not agree a sufficiently tough reform.
"It's a big step for Spain. It's not enough but let's see," Lumholdt said.
The main sticking point in the talks is the high dismissal costs for workers on permanent contracts, which employers say makes them reluctant to take on employees long term.
At the same time, unions are determined to solve the problem of contract instability that plagues Spain's labour market.
A Labour Ministry survey found that more than 96 percent of new jobs created in 1996 were temporary, and half of those were on contracts lasting less than a month.

Dolado recommends replacing current permanent unemployment benefits with one year's worth of benefits. Dismissal costs could be brought under control by making minimum severance agreements in each industry sector.
But even if reforms were to sweep aside these problems, the single currency poses at least one other risk for Spanish unemployment.
Demand must grow, but the new European Central Bank's greater devotion will likely be to prove its credentials as a defender of the currency and an inflation fighter.
"We are in dire straits," Dolado said. "The prospects are not optimistic."
